rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction once critical pairs are identified.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved separation while testing the critical pair's response to slope.

Both runs achieved the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient another step to locate the speed limit for full resolution. The critical pair is approaching R = 1.5, so this run will test whether further compression is viable at 40 C.

Keep the faster gradient and test whether higher temperature shifts selectivity enough to resolve the critical pair while further shortening retention. The 8-minute gradient at 40 C remains a fully resolved, maximum-CRF fallback.

Test the opposite temperature direction at the same gradient slope: cooling may widen the critical middle pair and avoid the early-pair co-elution seen at 60 C. Retention should still remain comfortably below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Narrow the gradient window to reduce steepness and recover middle-pair resolution without extending the programmed gradient. Use 50 C as a compromise between improved middle-pair selectivity and the early-pair co-elution observed at 60 C.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its slope to reduce retention and test starting-composition selectivity. Injection 6 provides a maximum-CRF fallback if the critical pair loses resolution.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while slightly reducing gradient steepness to protect the critical middle pair. This tests a faster separation without pushing temperature toward the early-pair co-elution region.

Continue raising the starting organic fraction one grid step while making the gradient slightly shallower. Monitor both early-peak retention and the critical middle pair as we seek a shorter separation that retains CRF 1.000.

Trim the gradient to the observed elution window and shorten its duration to 4 minutes. The shallower slope should help protect the middle pair as the higher starting organic fraction reduces retention; check that the early pair remains resolved.

Test a much steeper gradient to see whether the critical middle pair separates again after an elution-order reversal, enabling a substantially faster method. Lowering temperature to 40 C should help preserve early-pair separation; injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Keep the fast gradient and lower temperature to test whether cooling increases separation of the middle pair in this steep-gradient regime. This isolates temperature selectivity while checking that the late pair remains resolved.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to probe starting-composition selectivity of the middle pair. Cooling should help retain and separate the early compounds despite the stronger initial solvent; injection 10 remains the fastest maximum-CRF method.

Use a shallower gradient and moderately higher temperature than injection 13 to improve the critical middle pair. This tests whether the higher starting organic fraction can support full resolution without losing the early pair.

Increase the effective gradient slope slightly from injection 10, from 0.0875 to 0.0917 organic fraction per minute, to test its small resolution margin. Although the programmed gradient is longer, the steeper slope should bring the last peak out sooner.

Test whether 55 C permits a steeper, faster gradient by improving middle-pair selectivity. The lower starting organic fraction protects early retention, but early-pair resolution will determine whether this temperature is usable.

Return to 50 C to restore early-pair resolution and test a slope just steeper than injection 9. This targets a last-peak time near the fastest fully resolved result while probing the middle pair's resolution boundary.
Back off the slope from injection 17 by one endpoint step to restore full middle-pair resolution. This targets a short maximum-CRF method with more resolution margin than injection 10.

Preserve injection 18's successful slope through the critical middle pair, but end the gradient after 2 minutes. This tests whether a lower-organic hold can elute the last compounds promptly while retaining maximum CRF and reducing solvent use.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 10 to increase the critical middle pair's resolution margin while keeping the last peak inside the gradient. This targets a more robust maximum-CRF separation with only a modest retention-time increase.

Lower temperature one step from injection 20 to improve the early pair while testing whether the middle pair's resolution margin is sufficient. This explores a nearby maximum-CRF operating point; injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved method.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 21 to shorten retention while using its middle-pair resolution margin. Comparing this directly with injection 10 also tests whether the fastest fully resolved gradient tolerates a 5 C temperature decrease.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 18 to increase resolution margin while keeping all peaks comfortably below the time-penalty threshold. The maximum CRF is already secured; this run explores a less boundary-sensitive alternative to the fastest method, injection 10.

Test whether injection 18 retains full resolution after a one-step temperature decrease, using its middle-pair margin and stronger early retention. This evaluates a nearby maximum-CRF alternative while retaining injection 10 as the fastest fully resolved method.

Use a slope between injections 10 and 20 to target maximum CRF with slightly more resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method. All peaks should elute well before the gradient ends, with the last peak expected around 3.5 minutes.
